work-organization.text: Porcelain joined shaping, surface decoration, official designs, inspection and buying. Court supervision and private production could overlap; neither a reign mark nor a beautiful surface identifies every worker, a fulfilled commission or a particular customer.

audience.text: The catalogue places this jar in Jiajing-era ceramic production; the Ming essay documents a court Bureau of Design for imperial wares.

evidence.text: The vessel preserves material and decoration; it is not identified here as a specific galleon cargo.

name: Ming workshops and court design
geographicPrecision: Production center locator, not a boundary of artistic influence.

interval.label: 1368–1644 CE
interval.note: Conventional Ming dynastic period. Individual works and trade routes retain their own dates.

question: Who decided what a beautiful object should look like?
summary: Making Ming porcelain connected skilled surface work with designs, supervision and customers. Court orders mattered alongside private kilns and several markets. The selected fish jar makes materials inspectable, while changing production arrangements explain why a dynasty’s ceramics cannot be reduced to one style, maker or audience.

sections.title: A surface joins different kinds of work
sections.text: The fish jar combines a shaped porcelain body with decoration at different layers. The Met identifies cobalt painting beneath the glaze and coloured enamels above it. Look at how fish, plants and repeated borders fit the curved surface. Shaping, applying decoration and obtaining a finished vessel are connected tasks. The catalogue identifies the material and a broad production context; the photograph alone cannot reveal every technical step or name a maker. Pierson’s discussion of an official’s account follows quarried material through crushing, washing and preparation for shaping. Work began before the painted surface existed. Preparing usable material and controlling form made later decoration possible; a finished jar joins activities that a single photograph cannot separate.

citations.locator: Printed p. 12 / PDF 18: mediated preparation account

sections.title: An official order needed more than a design
sections.text: The court coordinated some decorative production through a Bureau of Design. The National Palace Museum describes models, appointed supervisors and selection of finished pieces for court use. Its early-Ming account includes both Longquan and Jingdezhen, rather than one city standing for all ceramics. Designs helped specify what to make, but production also required people to turn those requirements into objects. Official supervision was a relationship among institutions and workshops, not an explanation that removes the makers’ practical decisions.

sections.title: Inspection and buying linked different organizations
sections.text: The Palace Museum’s archaeological exhibition account describes inspection of imperial wares and disposal of rejected pieces. Such fragments matter alongside objects preserved in collections: they record selection as part of production. Private kilns also made porcelain. CUHK’s museum account explains that, during the Jiajing period, capable private producers could receive court orders beyond imperial capacity. Domestic buyers and overseas customers created other demand. Court and market work therefore cannot always be sorted into two isolated worlds.

sections.title: Demand and institutions changed
sections.text: The Palace Museum compares excavated fragments with surviving objects across the Jiajing, Longqing and Wanli reigns. It describes changing ranges of designs and reports imperial operations stopping in 1608, while private kilns continued. A change at the imperial works was not the end of pottery making. These shifts help answer who influenced an object’s appearance: patrons, administrators, buyers and skilled producers all enter the account. The selected jar remains a mid-sixteenth-century work, without an invented buyer, shipping route or complete workshop biography.

deeperReading.title: Selection changes the objects that survive
deeperReading.text: The Palace Museum brings production fragments into comparison with collected vessels. Its inspection account makes rejected and damaged wares part of the explanation, rather than treating an intact museum object as a complete record of making. Comparing these different survivals can test design classifications and production histories. The exhibition summaries do not provide a measured rejection rate or account for every object that circulated.

deeperReading.title: Related evidence does not identify a particular object
deeperReading.text: The Met mentions a 1542 order for similar pond-scene jars. A relationship of subject and period is useful without proving this jar belonged to that batch. Its technical account also draws on wear in comparable jars when explaining colour layers. Keep that comparative argument separate from a new analysis of this vessel. A reign mark helps frame attribution; it does not supply the names and experiences of all makers.

deeperReading.title: An institutional account is a question to investigate
deeperReading.text: The museum’s controlled-production account describes standards and permitted distribution. It does not establish that every instruction was followed. The market account adds contracted work and customers beyond the palace. Reading them together explains why private and official activities could intersect without identifying every transaction. Overseas sales also do not assign a particular voyage to every surviving pot. Further workshop, labor and commercial records are needed to explain conditions and changing bargaining power.

evidenceReading.title: A material identification, an account of work and a production history
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases. Visible colours, technical catalogue information, a translated official’s essay and archaeological comparisons have different purposes and limits.

items.label: The surface can be observed; its technique needs identification
items.text: The photograph shows fish, plants and borders on a rounded jar. The catalogue identifies underglaze cobalt and overglaze enamels, and cites records for similar jars in 1542.
items.interpretation: A visible pattern and technical attribution support different claims. The related order does not identify this jar’s batch, maker, customer or voyage; comparative colour evidence is not a newly performed assay of this object.

items.label: An official’s analogy is a purposeful account of work
items.text: Pierson presents Shao Bao’s description of preparation through Stephen Little’s translation. The official turns ceramic making into an analogy for moral development.
items.interpretation: This mediated viewpoint makes work discussable without becoming the speech of every worker, a chemical recipe or a measured schedule. The original Chinese edition and full translation source were not independently consulted.

items.label: Fragments and collected objects reveal selection and change
items.text: The Palace Museum compares excavated kiln material with collection objects and describes changes across three later-Ming reigns.
items.interpretation: A mixed archaeological and collection record helps investigate production. It does not measure all output or prove one uniform decline. The reported 1608 imperial stoppage must stay distinct from continuing private work.

familyActivity.title: A visible pattern, a question about making
steps: Point to one fish, one plant and one repeated border in the supplied photograph. Trace their arrangement in the air without counting the unseen side.
Read the source capsule together. Make cards for visible observation, technical identification and evidence about orders or buying.
Match “fish and plants fit around the body” and “cobalt lies under the glaze” to the right cards. Explain which needs the catalogue.
Write one supported statement and one question about the makers or buyer that the picture cannot answer.

The pictured arrangement can be observed. Its material identification uses catalogue research. Museum accounts describe court models, supervision, private kilns and several markets; they do not name this jar’s individual maker or buyer. A record for similar jars is not proof of this object’s batch or voyage.

review.reviewer: Codex selected institutional/scholarly source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian or craft specialist approval
review.scope: Layered inquiry into makers, supervision, markets and changes within Ming ceramic production. Selected official catalogue/essay rereads retain previous dated scopes; five new source records distinguish museum archaeological summaries and selected scholarly text. The entire original dynasty interval, identity, claims, earlier comparison meanings, object order and image bytes remain intact.
limitations: The complete 1368–1644 case, visible mid-sixteenth-century/Jiajing attribution, inherited 1534–1566 object search envelope and unknown camera date remain separate. No exact workshop foundation, firing day or completed batch assigned.

The Met’s 1542 reference concerns related jars and its colour explanation uses comparable examples. Original administrative order, new pigment analysis and present provenance-tab contents were not read. Direct local Met captures returned 429; actual exposed official web text was consulted without retrying another route.

Palace/National Palace Museum exhibition accounts are institutional syntheses, not complete field datasets or proof that all rules were enforced. Broad quality/quantity decline and universal private/imperial hierarchies are not adopted. The later 1681/1683 restart alternatives remain outside the Ming frame.

Pierson consultation is limited to selected printed pp. 9–12 and selected source notes; no full-book or original Chinese-text read, independent translation, exact workforce, wage, loss rate, working-day reconstruction or worker self-description claimed.

The CUHK market account does not identify this jar’s customer, shipment or route. No newly inferred contact with other workpack cases, geographic points, territorial borders or measured workshop plan supplied.

Existing jar pixels were actually inspected and retained. Remote-image parity and exposure date remain unverified. Source exhibition pictures and book figures are not copied or traced; no new visual asset or annotation promised.
Independent historical/craft and relevant community review, real family use, human screen-reader/physical-device behavior and physical print quality remain open.
